en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-śucinirdeśa-sūtra*, translator unknown; now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin.
In the past, the Buddha was traveling with Ānanda when they encountered a pond forty li from east to west.
It is forty *li* from north to south and forty *li* deep.
Within the pond there are insects whose shape resembles that of tadpoles, and their color is black like ink.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you recognize these insects in the pond?
He replied, "I do not recognize them."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"Those insects in this pool are the great assembly of the Saṃgha from the worlds of the ten directions who, having consumed impure food, have fallen into this foul and filthy pool of excrement. They shall constantly consume impurity and endure such suffering for five million lifetimes;
thereafter, for another five hundred lifetimes, they will again fall among hungry dogs, constantly consuming impurity."
Again he fell among swine, where for five hundred lifetimes he constantly ate filth;
again he fell among dung beetles, where he constantly ate filth.

After another five hundred lifetimes he emerged to become human, yet was always born into poor families; his clothing did not cover his body and his food did not suffice for his mouth; he constantly ate husks and rice bran, perpetually hungry and lacking enough.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Those who act in such a manner will undergo suffering for their transgressions that is most grievous, immeasurable, and boundless.
I warn you of future generations during the final dharma: all bhikṣus must be cautious; when there is a place where the entire saṃgha resides, one must not go to eat impure food."
Those who desire to purify their food should take only that which is entirely pure.

Their clothing and food must be in accordance with the Dharma; they should wear their robes and carry their alms bowls, maintaining the four dignified postures, and approach for alms in a manner consistent with the Dharma. Such a person is a true bhikṣu, one who has eliminated wrong livelihood and sustains his life in accordance with the Dharma.
“The Buddha does not speak falsely; the retribution of merit is like a shadow or an echo.
In the past, there was a bhikṣu who had newly attained arhatship; though he possessed a body bound by residual karma, he suffered from the ailment of needing to relieve himself.”
At night, while going to the latrine, he saw a bhikṣu groaning by the side of the latrine.
The arhat said to this bhikṣu, "You were originally a person who used his mind well; why have you fallen among the hungry ghosts and are groaning like this?"
The hungry ghost bhikṣu replied:

"I have suffered from hunger and thirst for a long time; for more than five hundred years, I have not seen even water or broth. I was just about to go to the latrine to consume its impurities when the yakṣa who guards the latrine struck me with an iron staff, preventing me from approaching it."

I recall that in the past, when I was a bhikṣu managing the affairs of the Saṃgha, I used impure food to come into contact with the pure food of the community and fed the Saṃgha with such impure food; therefore, this calamity has resulted.

If they encounter an Arhat as a virtuous friend, and that Arhat offers incense and recites prayers for the sake of the Bhikṣu-saṃgha, they will immediately escape the realm of hungry ghosts and return once more to the human path.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: "One must not be heedless;
no one at all shall touch the pure food of the Saṃgha. The Buddha does not speak falsely;
the retribution of merit is like a shadow or an echo. This is set forth in the *Sūtra on the Eighteen Hells* regarding transgressions and merits."

These hungry ghosts originally came from among human beings; they touched the pure vessels of the Sangha with impure hands, touched the pure food of the śramaṇas with impure hands, and placed impure food into the pure food of the śramaṇas.
Because he fed the Sangha impure food, for five hundred subsequent lifetimes he fell among the hungry ghosts (preta), constantly eating filth;
whenever he sought to go to a latrine to eat excrement, the deity of the latrine would seize him with an iron staff and beat him, preventing him from approaching.

This ghost feeds on human pus and blood, nasal mucus and saliva, as well as foul wash-water; it constantly watches for and seizes the impure blood from women’s childbirths to serve as its food and drink.
Furthermore, for five hundred lifetimes, they fell among pigs, dogs, and dung beetles, constantly eating foul excrement and impurities.

Undergoing such extreme suffering for successive generations in this manner, there was no prospect of escape for hundreds of thousands of kalpas; liberation was difficult to attain, and the pain was beyond description.
"Because one touched the male organ or the female organ with impure hands, touched the pure vessels of the śramaṇas, or touched the pure food of the śramaṇas;

because one placed impure food among the pure food of the śramaṇas, and fed the Saṃgha with impure food—one incurs this calamity. All people with their physical eyes do not know the distinction between sin and merit."

From this day forward, those who wish to obtain blessings and merit should assist the Sangha in preparing food; by handling the Sangha’s pure vessels with clean hands, washing the rice with clean hands, and placing the pure rice into the Sangha’s pure food, they shall obtain immeasurable merit.
From this day forward, let this be the constant rule, and let it be heard and known by all people:

whenever any donor establishes a Dharma assembly and provides the requisites for the offering and the fast, those who observe the fast shall receive food, while those who do not observe the fast shall not receive it.
If one observes the fast for a single day while eating this rice, one will obtain surplus provisions for six million lifetimes;
if one does not observe the fast, one will fall among the hungry ghosts for six million lifetimes. Why is this?
Because this food given out of faith is difficult to digest,
it would be better to swallow a red-hot iron ball than to eat this rice.

Swallowing a red-hot iron ball is but a momentary thing, whereas eating this food given out of faith leads to the endurance of great suffering for a long time— one undergoes the sufferings of a hungry ghost for five million lifetimes.
"In any place where food is prepared, all should perform the ritual according to the Dharma; one must not carry away leftover food to give to one's wife and children.
If one eats this rice, or carries it tucked under the arm, for five hundred subsequent lifetimes, one will constantly have a glowing iron wheel enter under the left armpit and emerge from the right."
"One must be extremely careful regarding all offerings for the fast; even a single grain of rice can transform into a hot pellet.

When all worthy ones establish a merit assembly, if one tastes this food beforehand, it becomes entirely 'leftover food' (vighasa). To hold such an assembly in vain is better than not holding it at all."
Why is this? The devas do not rejoice, and the spirits and deities do not delight.
Those who previously tasted [the food] from this person shall likewise undergo the suffering of hungry ghosts for five hundred lifetimes.

From this day forward, those who desire to obtain merit should prepare vegetarian offerings according to the Dharma; they shall thereby gain blessings and virtue, causing all the devas to rejoice and the hundred deities to celebrate, while the celestial gods provide them with protection.
"The scriptures do not speak falsely; the retribution of merit is like a shadow following a form or an echo following a sound.
Thus spoke the Buddha in the *Sūtra on Protecting Purity*.
